assistants.intro: An AI assistant is the place most people start: you type a question or task in plain English and it answers, writes, explains or plans. They all do the basics well, so the right one depends on what you use every day and what you need most.

picks.need: You live in Gmail, Docs and Android
You use Windows, Word and Outlook
Answers with sources you can check
Trying many AI models in one place

howTo: Start with the assistant that fits the apps you already use. Built-in beats switching apps.
Give each one the same real task from your week (an email, a summary, a plan) and compare the answers.
If you need facts, pick one that shows sources, and click them. All assistants can be confidently wrong.
Check the privacy settings before pasting anything personal or confidential. Most let you turn off training on your chats.
Use the free plan for a week before paying. Upgrade only if you keep hitting the limits.

faq.q: Which AI assistant is the best?
faq.a: There's no single best. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all strong all-rounders. Pick the one that fits the apps you already use, then test it on a few real tasks from your week.

faq.q: Are AI assistants free?
faq.a: Most have a free plan that's enough for everyday use. Paid plans add higher limits, newer models and extra features.

faq.q: Can I trust what an AI assistant tells me?
faq.a: Treat answers like advice from a smart friend: usually helpful, sometimes wrong. Check anything important, especially facts, numbers, medical, legal or money questions.

writing.intro: AI writing tools range from simple grammar checkers to full writers that draft emails, posts and articles. Most people need one checker that fixes their own writing, and maybe one assistant for first drafts.

picks.need: Fixing grammar and tone as you type
Rewriting a sentence that sounds wrong
Writing in more than one language

howTo: Decide if you want help fixing your own words (a checker) or someone to draft for you (a writer). They're different tools.
Pick one that works where you write: browser, Word, Google Docs or your email app.
Always read and edit AI drafts. Readers notice generic, robotic writing.
For work writing, check whether the tool keeps or trains on your text.
If you write in more than one language, test each language before paying.

faq.q: What is the best AI tool for writing emails?
faq.a: For fixing your own emails, Grammarly or Wordtune. For drafting emails from scratch, a general assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude works well. Superhuman builds AI writing into the email app itself.

faq.q: Can teachers or readers tell if writing is AI-generated?
faq.a: Often, yes. AI drafts tend to sound generic. Use AI for a first draft or for polishing, then add your own words, examples and opinions.

faq.q: Is a grammar checker enough?
faq.a: For most people, yes. A good checker fixes mistakes and unclear sentences without changing your voice.

career.intro: AI career tools help with the three hardest parts of job hunting: a resume that gets past screening software, a cover letter that matches the job, and practice before the interview.

picks.need: Matching your resume to a job ad

howTo: Fix the resume first. Use a matching tool to compare it against each job ad and add the missing skills you really have.
Never let AI invent experience. Recruiters check, and it can cost you the job.
Tailor every cover letter to the company. A generic AI letter is easy to spot.
Practise interview answers out loud with an AI coach, then with a real person.
Use a tracker once you're applying to more than a few jobs, so nothing slips.

faq.q: Do AI resume builders really help you get interviews?
faq.a: They help most with format and keywords, so applicant tracking systems can read your resume. The content still has to be true and specific to you.

faq.q: What is an applicant tracking system (ATS)?
faq.a: Software that companies use to sort and filter resumes before a person reads them. Clear formatting and the right keywords from the job ad help your resume get through.

faq.q: Is it OK to use AI for a cover letter?
faq.a: Yes, as a starting draft. Then rewrite it in your own words with real examples, so it doesn't sound generic.

design.intro: AI design tools can make images from a sentence, clean up photos, and produce logos and social posts in minutes. The right tool depends on whether you need art, business graphics or photo fixes.

picks.need: Images with readable text in them
Images that are safer for business use

howTo: Decide what you're making: a picture (image generator), a design (Canva-style editor) or a photo fix (editing tool).
For anything commercial, read the tool's terms on who owns the images and whether you can use them in ads.
Be specific in your prompt: subject, style, colours, mood and layout.
Make several versions and pick the best. Small prompt changes make big differences.
Check hands, faces and text in AI images before you publish. Mistakes are common.

faq.q: Can I use AI images for my business?
faq.a: Often yes, but it depends on the tool's terms and your plan. Adobe Firefly is designed with commercial use in mind. Always check the license before using images in ads or products.

faq.q: What is the easiest AI design tool for beginners?
faq.a: Canva. It has templates for almost everything and AI features built in, so you don't start from a blank page.

faq.q: Can AI make a good logo?
faq.a: AI logo makers are good for quick, simple logos and ideas. For a brand you'll use for years, consider having a designer refine the result.

video.intro: AI video and audio tools can edit video by editing text, add captions automatically, generate clips from a description, and create natural voices and music. Most people only need one editor plus one specialist tool.

picks.need: Turning long videos into short clips

howTo: Start from your goal: editing your own footage, generating new video, or making voice and music.
For social media, pick a tool with auto captions and vertical (9:16) export.
Generated video is great for short shots and ideas, but still struggles with long, consistent scenes.
Only clone a voice or use a face with that person's clear permission.
Check the license before using AI music or voices in videos you earn money from.

faq.q: What is the easiest AI video editor?
faq.a: CapCut and Descript are both beginner-friendly. Descript is especially easy for talking videos, because you edit the video by editing the transcript.

faq.q: Can AI make a full video from text?
faq.a: Tools like Runway, Pika and Luma can generate short clips from text or images. For complete videos with a presenter, tools like Synthesia and HeyGen work better.

faq.q: Is it legal to use AI voices and music?
faq.a: It depends on the tool's license and on consent. Use voices you have rights to, and check the music license before commercial use.

work.intro: AI work tools take care of the busywork: meeting notes, scheduling, slides and repetitive tasks between apps. One good notetaker and one automation tool can save hours every week.
howTo: Start with your biggest time-waster this week (meetings, scheduling or copying data between apps) and fix that one first.
Check that the tool works with what you already use: Zoom, Google Meet or Teams; Google or Outlook calendar.
Always tell people when a meeting is being recorded. In some places it's required by law.
For automation, start with one small, boring task and grow from there.
Review AI meeting summaries before sending them to others.

faq.q: What is the best AI notetaker for meetings?
faq.a: Otter.ai, Fireflies.ai, Fathom and tl;dv all record and summarise calls. Pick the one that works with your meeting app and fits your budget.

faq.q: Is it OK to record meetings with AI?
faq.a: Only with the other people's knowledge. Many tools announce themselves, but you should still tell people, and some places legally require consent.

faq.q: Zapier or Make: which is easier?
faq.a: Zapier is usually easier for beginners. Make gives more control over complex, multi-step automations.

business.intro: AI tools for small businesses help you get a website live, answer customers around the clock, and run marketing without a big team. Start with the one that brings in customers or saves the most time.

picks.need: A flexible site with lots of templates
A polished site or online store
A support chatbot trained on your site

howTo: Get the basics right first: a clear website with your services, prices, location and contact details.
Choose a builder you can update yourself. You'll change things more often than you think.
If customers ask the same questions, a chatbot trained on your own website can answer them 24/7.
Make sure AI chatbots hand off to a real person for complaints and complicated questions.
Check that AI search tools can find and describe your business correctly. Ask ChatGPT or Perplexity about your business and see what comes back.

faq.q: Can AI build a website for my business?
faq.a: Yes. Durable, Wix and Hostinger can generate a first version in minutes from a short description. You should still edit the text and add real photos.

faq.q: Should my small business use an AI chatbot?
faq.a: If you get lots of repeat questions, yes. Train it on your own website and FAQ, and make sure customers can easily reach a person.

faq.q: How do I get ChatGPT to recommend my business?
faq.a: Have a clear website that explains what you do and where, consistent business details across the web, and real reviews. AI assistants rely on the same public information people do.

build.intro: No-code AI builders let you describe an app in plain English and get a working version, without being a programmer. They're great for prototypes, internal tools and simple products.

picks.need: A web app from a chat description
Prompting and deploying in the browser
Building and hosting with an AI agent
Turning a spreadsheet into an app
A complex web app without code

howTo: Write down what the app must do in 5 to 10 plain sentences before you start. Clear instructions give better apps.
Start small: build one screen that works, then add features one at a time.
Check where your data is stored and whether you can export it or the code later.
Be careful with logins, payments and personal data. Get a developer to review anything handling money or private information.
Watch usage-based pricing. Costs can grow as you use more AI credits.

faq.q: Can I really build an app without coding?
faq.a: Yes, for many simple apps, prototypes and internal tools. Complex apps with lots of users or sensitive data usually still need a developer.

faq.q: Lovable, Bolt or Replit: which should I try first?
faq.a: All three build working apps from a description. Try the same small idea in each for an hour and keep the one whose result you like best.

faq.q: Do I own the app I build?
faq.a: Usually yes, but check each tool's terms, and whether you can export your code or data if you leave.

developer.intro: AI coding tools range from autocomplete in your editor to agents that plan changes, edit many files and run tests. Most developers use one in-editor assistant plus one agent for bigger tasks.

picks.need: Open source, bring your own model
If you use IntelliJ or PyCharm

howTo: Try it on your real codebase, not a demo. Results vary a lot by language and project size.
Decide how much control you want: suggestions you accept line by line, or an agent that makes larger changes for you to review.
Check your company's rules on sending code to outside AI services before you start.
Review every change and keep tests running. AI code can look right and still be wrong.
Compare total cost per developer, including usage-based charges for agents.

faq.q: What is the best AI coding assistant?
faq.a: It depends on your editor and workflow. Cursor and GitHub Copilot are popular in-editor choices, and Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI are popular coding agents.

faq.q: Is AI-written code safe to use?
faq.a: Only after review. Treat it like code from a new team member: read it, test it, and check for security issues.

faq.q: Will my code be used to train AI models?
faq.a: It depends on the tool and plan. Business plans usually offer stronger privacy terms. Check the settings and terms before using AI on private code.

learn.intro: AI learning tools explain hard topics simply, help you study and practise, and find and summarise research. Used well, they're like a patient tutor that's always available.

picks.need: Asking questions about your own documents
What the science says on a question
Speaking practice in a new language

howTo: Use AI to explain and quiz you, not to do the work for you. You remember what you practise.
For school or university, check your teacher's or institution's rules on AI use.
For research, use tools that link to real papers, and open the papers to check.
Upload your own notes or textbooks to get answers based on what you're actually studying.
For languages, practise speaking out loud. Conversation practice builds confidence fastest.

faq.q: What is the best AI tool for studying?
faq.a: Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) is great for studying your own notes and readings. Quizlet is good for flashcards, and Khanmigo works as a tutor for school subjects.

faq.q: Can AI find real research papers?
faq.a: Yes. Elicit, Consensus, Semantic Scholar and Scite search real academic papers. Always open the paper itself before citing it.

faq.q: Is using AI for homework cheating?
faq.a: It depends on the rules of your class. Using AI to explain ideas or quiz yourself is usually fine. Handing in AI-written work as your own usually isn't.
